title: What this means inside a lambda and inside an anonymous class

blocks.text: A lambda does not open a scope of its own: inside its body, `this` is the object of the enclosing class. An anonymous inner class is a new object, so `this` inside it is that anonymous object. A lambda may also update the enclosing object's **fields**, because they belong to the object, not to the method.
`Tally` holds an `int count` field (read with `count()`). Write three methods:

items: `incrementer()` returns a `Runnable` lambda that adds one to `count` each time it runs.
`selfFromLambda()` returns a `Supplier<Object>` written **as a lambda** whose body is just `this`.
`selfFromAnonymousClass()` returns a `Supplier<Object>` written **as an anonymous inner class** whose `get()` returns `this`.

blocks.text: The tests check which object each `this` turns out to be.

cases.says: Each run of an incrementer adds one to the tally's own count field.
Inside a lambda, this is the enclosing Tally, not the lambda.
Inside an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object itself, not the Tally.
Two incrementers made from one tally both add to the same field; neither keeps a private copy of the count.
